Minor gameplay tweak

notes.title: Self Defence on Marzanna
notes.content:
Though combat is not the focus of Abject Abyss, you can still find ways of defending yourself in a pinch.


[img src="{STEAM_CLAN_IMAGE}/45313576/000dcd66ba263a1264407449215fc5f7264dbf7d.png"]



The Shock Pistol is a non-lethal weapon used by security officers, but for Ernest it’s a way to temporarily disable enemies and buy time to escape.



Ammunition is limited, -one capsule is one shot- but it's accurate and has a decent range. Hitting an enemy will root them in place as they squirm violently under the electrical current, the heat causing smoke to rise from sizzling flesh.



If you happen to have several capsules saved you can keep firing to greatly extend the duration of the shock, disorienting and burning the target. It wont stop them, not permanently. But it will give you enough time to run or hide.



It's also important to note that you cannot interact while the pistol is drawn, so it’s best to only bring it out when you really need it, then stow it as you make your escape. Another tool in Ernest’s belt. 



Of course the best outcome would be never needing the Shock Pistol at all, but having the option might help you feel a little safer... as long as you still have a capsule left.

notes.title: Demo update 0.2.5
notes.content:
Updated Demo build to 0.2.5

Made the glow-rod movement a little more dynamic. Reacts to jumping now etc.

Moved the FOV slider into display settings. I don’t know why I had it in controls.

Added a setting to turn tutorial messages off or on.

If tutorials are on, the first chase will prompt the player to run.

The monster’s footsteps are also louder in the chase.

Added a new item to the Security level as a tease.

Slightly changed inventory art for improved powercells.

Added a button to the main menu that links to the presskit.

Footsteps are now louder when landing after jumping/falling instead of sometimes being very quiet even after a long fall.

notes.title: Demo update 0.2.4

notes.title: Demo Launch
notes.content:
The Demo is out now!
At long last, the demo is public on steam.  It contains the first 30-60 minutes of the game, enough to give you a solid idea of what to expect.

 

And as a bonus, saves from the demo will carry over in the full game, letting you pick up right where you left off at release.

Details
This is the first part of the game in it's current state. I'm sure there will be further tweaks and modifications, but what you play in the demo is mostly the same thing a new player at release would get.


The demo will be kept up to date with the full game at least until release, and I do intended to leave the demo up after launch. That way people can try the game free for a while to see if they're interested before having to spend any money.


Bugs?
I've ironed out a lot of bugs so far, but if you happen to discover a new one, there is a button in the pause menu that links to a bug-report form. 



(There are still a few issues for some people using a controller in certain menus. It seems to vary.)


How's the full game going?
It's going well! On the one hand, I still have so much left to do and release seems so far away. But on the other, everything's coming together relatively smoothly and I'm enjoying the process. 

I can't say for sure if I'll reach my goal of a 2025 release, but I do think the bulk of the work is behind me, which is a good feeling!





Thanks to everyone who plays or wishlists, I'll see you in the next update!

notes.title: Closed Playtesting
notes.content:
The first playtest build of Abject Abyss is nearly ready!
Right now, there is still time to sign up to be one of the first testers, but the cut off will be soon. (Though you can still join the mailing list after and potentially gain access to later events.)

Note: playtesting signups have now closed. 


What will the playtest include?
It'll be the first part of the game, the same section that will eventually become the public demo. It's got all the basic elements of the game, enough to give people an idea of what the rest will be like.


How long will it take until the demo is released?
It'll depend on how many problems the playtesting uncovers. I want to at least get all the major issues handled before the public demo, because you know that demo's gonna reveal even more.

But even worst case scenario, I reckon it wont be too long before something gets out to the public.


How long exactly is the demo?
That's one of the things I'm hoping to find out through these tests. I know how long it makes me to play through these levels. But I'm the developer. 

It's so hard to know how other people are going to interact with what you've made. But after this test, I should have a much better idea.


That's all for now
Now I need to get back to work. The last little bit always seems to take the longest.

Consider following me on bluesky if you want a more sporadic source of small updates.

notes.title: Making Monsters
notes.content:
A horror game doesn’t necessarily need any monsters in it. That said, Abject Abyss has several.

If you have any experience with game dev, this wont be anything new to you. But for everyone else I hope it’ll be an interesting peak into the process of building a game ready character from scratch.

Now, I personally prefer to go into a new horror game as blind as possible, without knowing what kind of terrors to expect. Things are often scarier the less you know after all. With that in mind, I don’t want to reveal too much about what you’ll encounter in the game, so I’ll only be using a single enemy as an example. One from the early game that you’ll encounter very briefly, and will be present in the demo. That way the rest remains a surprise.

If you really want to go in entirely blind and spoiler free, you can skip this update for now. Otherwise, lets continue.

{STEAM_CLAN_IMAGE}/45313576/269b067eabfeb6c24067a4006cec003d69247711.png
Concepts
This is an early game enemy. The idea is to show a person in a sort of metamorphosis. They are in the process of becoming something different, but haven't quite got there yet.
I generally start sketching out ideas with a pencil as I have them, then go digital for further development. I’ve got an old Wacom Cintiq from many years ago that’s somehow still functioning, which I use for painting.

Being a solo-dev really makes this phase much faster. I pretty much start knowing what I want, and with no other conflicting opinions I can get a design finalised very quickly.

{STEAM_CLAN_IMAGE}/45313576/303608d8e9e0195288299428f9a0e72d8ba0aaf7.png
Modelling
The next step is modelling the thing.

Making the base mesh isn’t too hard. Start with a cube, extrude it out, add subdivisions, move those verts around. It’s more tedious than difficult.

This particular monster is asymmetrical, which is a little annoying because it prevents me from mirroring some of the skin weights later on, but I’m the one who designed it this way so I can’t complain.

Quick sidetrack on modelling software
I don’t think the program used matters that much, but I’ll point this one out because I differ from most indie devs here in that I’m using Maya. Blender’s a perfectly good program —Not to mention free—, but Maya is what I learned to use back when I studied this stuff, so it’s what I’m comfortable with. Being comfortable with your tools is important. It’s the same reason I’m using Unreal Engine, because I started learning in UDK and it was easy to transfer those skills.
	Anyway, back to making a monster;

{STEAM_CLAN_IMAGE}/45313576/662ab90a21b11521679fe4ba294de1563365fb84.png
Texturing/Sculpting
Once the base mesh is ready to go, it’s time to add those gross details. First is a high detail mesh with all the little bumps and fleshy wrinkles that will be used to create a normal map for the in-game model.

Then I paint the textures on. I’m painting colours, but also roughness information and extra fine normal detail. Making some parts look a little wetter than others, that kind of thing.

The full material comes together in Unreal, but at this point most of the work is done.

{STEAM_CLAN_IMAGE}/45313576/80f9ceb9c351021d094907543a04773291c73b27.png
Rigging
Back in Maya, It’s time to put the bones in.

I hate this part. 

Essentially, I’m putting a joint inside the model at each point that it needs to be able to move. Then I have to create controls and attach them to the bones so I can animate them. And when that’s done, I need to actually skin the mesh onto the bones so it deforms correctly when it moves.

It is an extremely tedious process and I hate doing it every time. Professional riggers out there, you have my respect.

The good thing about rigging gross monsters, is that you can get away with the deformation not being perfect. It’s already a twisted mass of flesh so if it moves a little wonky it’ll just add to the effect.(within reason)

{STEAM_CLAN_IMAGE}/45313576/9357f8878245f4ab6478dea27ecaa62875a43f30.png
Animating
Once it’s all rigged I can start making animations.

I start with a few idle animations. Doing these helps me get a feel for how the creature should move. I make a basic one, then a few with more movement and character that can play randomly.

Then I do movement. Different speeds of walking and running, and variations for turning.

Last is the attack animations. These are going to be blended on top of the movement, so I’m only animating from the pelvis up. For this guy, his attack options are pretty limited, so I only did two variations.

All in all the animations could do with more polish, but there’s only so much time I can spend on a single enemy. Can’t be a perfectionist when your a solo dev.

{STEAM_CLAN_IMAGE}/45313576/c79ea982f80983e20eeeebf46c260353eed8ba76.png
Sounds
The last thing I need to do before putting it all together, is make the sounds.

For the vocals I recorded my own voice with a hand over my mouth, and then filtered the crap out of the recordings until it sounded the way I imagined.

For movement, I mixed a bunch of leather stretching noises, with the sounds of fruit being squished. I made variations for different speeds of movement, as well as some bare-foot walking sounds. In unreal I set all these up in sound-cues with random variations in pitch and volume each time they play.

{STEAM_CLAN_IMAGE}/45313576/02a20a2c959598aea811b7872d3af849e2996fad.png
Importing
Now it’s time to get everything all hooked up together in Unreal!

The skeletal mesh first, then the materials. Then I set up the character and it’s animation blueprint.

The animBP determines what animations to play at any given time. These can get pretty complicated but this one is fairly basic. I did add some additive animations so he leans when cornering or accelerating/decelerating, but that’s just for me. I doubt most people would notice, but when it’s absent *I* notice.

I also hook up those sounds I made to the animations using notifies in Unreal. Little tags that let the engine know to play certain sounds at specific points in each animation.

The vocalisations trigger at random intervals, but it’ll pick from a list of them based on the monsters state, so it sounds more aggressive when chasing you than it does wandering around.

{STEAM_CLAN_IMAGE}/45313576/d70e43724760dc036ad5cf685ad0d16034ad07c5.png
Behaviour
Then comes the brain. I set up a character, and an AI controller with vision and hearing perceptions. Then I build a behaviour tree to control the monster’s actions.

I’m not going to show the actual tree here, I want to keep the enemies inner workings a little mysterious. Even if this one is very basic.

He can patrol around, investigate sounds, and give chase if he sees the player. Classic stealth game stuff.

Even this simple behaviour had a lot of bugs when I first implemented it. I think I’ve ironed most of them out, but we’ll see.

This foundation is the base for most monsters, but they do each have their own unique behaviour trees built on top of it.

{STEAM_CLAN_IMAGE}/45313576/14f80740fb3069eed2240b507641ee9991732353.png
Wrap Up
That’s how the monster gets made. From there it’s a whole lot of small tweaks and bug fixes, just like everything else.

Hopefully you found this interesting. And hopefully you still find this guy scary in-game despite the behind the scenes look. If not, at least the others should still be a surprise! 

Anyway, I’ve gotta get back to work. 
	See you next time!

notes.title: Finding Items and Filling Inventories
notes.content:
{STEAM_CLAN_IMAGE}/45313576/dfdde507305b24f47dce7a772c2826e16a6c9d71.jpg

Adventure games usually involve collecting items and adding them to your inventory. Beyond key items for puzzles, depending on the game, you may find consumable items and resources too.

This is especially true for horror. How many games have you searching every nook and cranny for flashlight batteries that inexplicably run dry in about 5 minutes each?

For Abject Abyss, I knew exploration needed rewards. What would be the point of finding a secret area if it was empty? It took a bit of brainstorming but I settled on a few different ideas.


POWER CELLS
{STEAM_CLAN_IMAGE}/45313576/e2a809ae29699305fd9a039fd0676e280d1d2d17.jpg
I know what you're thinking, and no, this is not a battery.
I decided against putting a typical horror flashlight in Abject Abyss. Instead, the player can find a small extendable glow rod as their mobile light source. It emits a dim glow around them, but the light doesn't penetrate very far ahead. 
Fuel for your light source is a good idea for a consumable item, there's a reason so many do it. But I wanted the glow rod to be an endless source of light, in return for its diminished range and power compared to a flashlight.

But I figured I could still give players a pick up that related to it.

The result? Finding an improved power cell for the glow rod permanently boosts its brightness and range.

That's a pretty good upgrade, so it's also very rare. You'll only encounter two or three of these in a playthrough.

STIM PENS
{STEAM_CLAN_IMAGE}/45313576/c61cad7c39ce0ee56ffb911da3046cb1772f295e.jpg
The classic sci-fi healing item. Inject yourself with liquid goo and watch as those wounds start closing up!
There is some lore in the game about how they work, but mechanically this is just a different flavor of med-kit.

It's not a full heal, You'd need a few of these to get from 'barely breathing' back up to max health, but they are also the most common consumable you'll find.

SUPPLEMENTS
{STEAM_CLAN_IMAGE}/45313576/07415e9049de56641b0161e3798cc1db2e85d1c8.jpg
Bottle'o pills. Using one of these will also give you a solid bit of healing (though less than the stim), but the real benefit they offer is a permanent increase in vitality. 

it's a small incremental increase, but if you're a good explorer finding all of them, it really adds up towards the end. Especially considering how much more dangerous the enemies get.

Of course, extra health only matters if you're taking damage. It'd be better to stay hidden from danger, or if needed, to run.
Which brings me to the next item:

ENERGY DRINKS
{STEAM_CLAN_IMAGE}/45313576/83ba7d2c68051600e70e39f491b14a3833a6e122.jpg
Yep, it's an energy drink! (Zero sugar too, for those worried about calories.)

Like the supplements, these offer a little healing (the least of the bunch) but also a nice permanent stat increase. 

You might've been able to guess which; speed. If a monster gets you in their sights, having chugged a few cans might the deciding factor in whether or not you get away.


IS THAT ALL OF THEM?

The rest of the items are more directly tied to story, puzzles, and progression. These are all the little extras you might find if you're being observant.

I'll be back in the new year with another update. Until then, I hope you have a great holiday season!

notes.title: Abject Abyss Announced!
notes.content:
Now that Abject Abyss is on steam, I'd like to take a moment to give some context beyond what's shown in the screenshots and trailers, and some info about myself.

What kind of Horror?
There is an abundance of indie horror games these days, which I'm happy to see. I love seeing different developer's spins on ideas and themes, and all the weird sub-genres that pop up as a result. I enjoy a lot of different types of horror, but Horror-Adventure is where my heart truly lies, and that's where Abject Abyss falls too.

The Horror part you already know. Thick atmosphere, eerie sounds, creepy visuals, and of course monsters roaming around that must be avoided. But what about the Adventure in Horror-Adventure?
Let me mention a few key things I mean:


An inventory
Collecting items, door keys, healing items, etc.
A world
No one likes having lore forcibly dumped on them, but if there's nothing there at all you can really feel the absence. Finding notes and audio logs may be cliché, but it's cliché for a reason. I personally love finding little tidbits of lore and story scattered across a game. And if you don't? It's not like reading is compulsory.
Obstacles/Puzzles
I don't mean putting yet another Tower of Hanoi puzzle into a room. But finding something in your way and using a little brain power (or your inventory) to overcome it. Otherwise you'd just be walking through hallways occasionally running from a monster. Which is fine, but I like things feeling more involved than just a haunted house ride.
A sense of progress
This is the big one. There are some fantastic horrors that take place exclusively in one incredibly detailed area, but I've always loved reaching the end of a game and really feeling like I've covered a lot of ground. Like it was an actual journey, in a physical sense.

That's just my personal taste of course. But it should help give you an idea of what kind of game I intend to make.

I'll talk more about all the monsters and spooky stuff later.

Who's Making this game?
Hey, I'm Anton. I'm a New Zealand based developer with a background in art and animation.

Have you made anything before this?
Yes, and you can check some of that out over on my Itch page: https://antonbezett.itch.io/

Those games were all made in an incredibly short time frame, take a few minutes to play, and are leaning into the 'PSX' graphic style (Chosen entirely because of how fast it is to make assets for). 

Abject Abyss is going to be quite different to any of those, but feel free to have a gander if you're interested. It's all free.

What's next?
I'm currently hard at work on the Abject Abyss Demo. I'm not ready to announce a release date just yet,   but progress is steady. I'll let you know when it's close.
Thanks!
